Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow. This is Macbeth's bleak soliloquy after learning of Lady Macbeth's death, in which he articulates the meaninglessness of life and the futility of human striving.

Macbeth speaks in Act V as his ambition crumbles around him. He begins with the repetition that defines the speech: tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace from day to day. The very rhythm conveys tedium, the mechanical passage of time that stretches endlessly into insignificance. Macbeth describes life as a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. Existence is mere noise and spectacle, devoid of meaning.

This reflection marks Macbeth's psychological collapse. He has murdered to seize power, yet all of it feels hollow and purposeless. The play's opening obsession with ambition inverts entirely—Macbeth now sees all striving as vanity. Out, out, brief candle, he cries, describing life as a fragile, short-lived light extinguished by death. The speech reveals that his own choices may have been predetermined illusions, that fate has rendered his agency meaningless. It is a Shakespearean articulation of pure nihilism, as the tyrant transforms from ambitious usurper into a nihilist prophet of emptiness.
